/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern builder
 * @options 7cd4d8193d7d35fe
 */

/**
 * A field of `Target`: its string keys.
 *
 * Narrowed to strings rather than being `keyof Target` because every name here
 * ends up in a message or a required-field list, and a symbol-keyed field has
 * no name to put in one. A target holding such a field can still be built —
 * that field is simply not one this builder sets.
 */
export type OrderField<Target> = Extract<keyof Target, string>;

/**
 * The one thing that can go wrong: `build` was reached with required fields
 * unset.
 *
 * `missing` is sorted, so two builders given the same required fields in
 * different orders report them identically.
 */
export interface OrderBuildFailure {
  readonly missing: readonly string[];
}

/**
 * The failure as a sentence, for a log line or a response body.
 *
 * Singular and plural are separated because a message reading “Missing required
 * fields: recipient.” is the kind of detail that makes generated code look
 * generated.
 */
export function describeOrderBuildFailure(failure: OrderBuildFailure): string {
  const fields = failure.missing.join(", ");
  return failure.missing.length === 1
    ? `Missing required field: ${fields}.`
    : `Missing required fields: ${fields}.`;
}

/**
 * Raised by `build` when a required field was never set.
 *
 * The missing fields are a property as well as being in the message, because a
 * handler that wants to report them should not have to parse its own error
 * text.
 */
export class OrderBuildError extends Error {
  readonly missing: readonly string[];

  constructor(failure: OrderBuildFailure) {
    super(describeOrderBuildFailure(failure));
    this.name = "OrderBuildError";
    this.missing = failure.missing;
  }
}

/**
 * `OrderBuilder`: a value under construction, checked when it is built.
 *
 * There is one type parameter rather than three, because nothing here is
 * tracked in the type: the fields that must be present are a run-time list, and
 * `build` compares it against what it has.
 *
 * Which is the rendering to reach for when the fields are not known statically
 * — a form submission, a CSV header, a config file. The typestate rendering can
 * prove more, and cannot help at all when the keys arrive as strings.
 */
export interface OrderBuilder<Target> {
  /**
   * Sets a field, returning a builder that has it.
   *
   * The value is typed `Target[K]`, so the key and the value are still checked
   * against each other — that much a type can do here. What it cannot do is
   * track *which* keys were set, which is what the typestate rendering is for
   * and why this one takes the required fields as a value.
   */
  set<K extends OrderField<Target>>(
    key: K,
    value: Target[K],
  ): OrderBuilder<Target>;

  /**
   * Assembles the value, checking that every required field was set.
   *
   * Raises `OrderBuildError` naming the fields that were never set.
   */
  build(): Target;
}

/**
 * An empty builder for `Target`, waiting on `required`.
 *
 * The list is a value here, which is the point of this rendering: the fields
 * that will arrive are not known when this code is compiled, so the check
 * cannot be either.
 *
 * Sorted once, on the copy this makes rather than on the caller's array, so
 * every failure reports its fields in the same order however the list was
 * written.
 */
export function createOrderBuilder<Target>(
  required: readonly OrderField<Target>[],
): OrderBuilder<Target> {
  return step([...required].sort(), {});
}

/**
 * A builder seeded from a value that is already complete, for editing one field
 * of it.
 *
 * No required list is needed: a value of type `Target` has every field `Target`
 * requires, and no step can remove one, so `build` cannot fail here. It is
 * still typed as though it could, since the type has no way to say that this
 * builder is the one that started full.
 *
 * The value is copied rather than held, so the original is unaffected by what
 * follows.
 */
export function createOrderBuilderFrom<Target>(
  value: Target,
): OrderBuilder<Target> {
  return step([], { ...(value as Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>) });
}

/**
 * One rung of the ladder: the required fields, the accumulated ones, and the
 * methods between them.
 *
 * Every method returns a fresh call to this rather than mutating `values`, so
 * two callers branching off one builder cannot interfere.
 *
 * `Object.hasOwn` rather than a check against `undefined`, for two reasons. A
 * field explicitly set to `undefined` is a decision the caller made and the
 * compiler already vetted, and reading it back as unset would quietly overrule
 * both. And `key in values` — the other spelling that reaches for — walks the
 * prototype chain, so a field named `toString` would count as provided by every
 * object that ever existed.
 */
function step<Target>(
  required: readonly string[],
  values: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>>,
): OrderBuilder<Target> {
  return {
    set(key, value) {
      return step<Target>(required, { ...values, [key]: value });
    },

    build() {
      const missing = required.filter((key) => !Object.hasOwn(values, key));

      if (missing.length > 0) {
        throw new OrderBuildError({ missing });
      }

      return { ...values } as Target;
    },
  };
}

## order-builder-example.ts (example)

```ts
/**
 * @generated by patterns — regenerate rather than edit.
 * @pattern builder
 * @options 7cd4d8193d7d35fe
 */

import {
  OrderBuildError,
  createOrderBuilder,
  createOrderBuilderFrom,
} from "./order-builder.js";

/**
 * The value being assembled.
 *
 * `note` being optional is why it is absent from the required list below: the
 * list says what `build` waits for, and an optional field is not that.
 */
export interface ShipmentLabel {
  readonly trackingId: string;
  readonly recipient: string;
  readonly note?: string;
}

/**
 * Fields arriving as strings, which is what the checked rendering is for.
 *
 * The keys here are `string` at run time — a form field, a CSV column, a config
 * key — so no type could have tracked which of them turned up. The required
 * fields are therefore a list, given in whatever order reads best, and `build`
 * reports the ones that never arrived.
 *
 * The list is not in alphabetical order on purpose: the failure sorts it, so a
 * message never depends on how this literal was written.
 */
export function labelFrom(
  entries: readonly (readonly [string, string])[],
): ShipmentLabel {
  let builder = createOrderBuilder<ShipmentLabel>(["trackingId", "recipient"]);

  for (const [key, value] of entries) {
    if (key === "trackingId" || key === "recipient" || key === "note") {
      builder = builder.set(key, value);
    }
  }

  return builder.build();
}

/**
 * The same entries, answered as a sentence.
 *
 * The error carries the missing fields as well as naming them, so a handler
 * that wants to list them does not have to read its own message.
 */
export function describeLabel(
  entries: readonly (readonly [string, string])[],
): string {
  try {
    const label = labelFrom(entries);
    return `${label.trackingId} for ${label.recipient}`;
  } catch (error) {
    if (error instanceof OrderBuildError) {
      return error.message;
    }
    throw error;
  }
}

/**
 * Changing one field of a finished value.
 *
 * Nothing can be missing from a value that already has the type, so this build
 * cannot fail — though it is still shaped as though it could, since the type
 * cannot say which builders started full.
 */
export function readdressed(
  existing: ShipmentLabel,
  recipient: string,
): ShipmentLabel {
  return createOrderBuilderFrom(existing).set("recipient", recipient).build();
}
```
